Dunning-Kruger effect and how we approach feminism

I'm going to go ahead and disagree with some of what you're saying.

So OK, you're educated in a STEM field. So the thing about STEM fields is that they teach reality as we understand it and are open to new ideas. If you start talking about the theory of relativity or Ohm's Law, people don't get to argue with you. The science is done. You can talk about the latest and greatest and are able to freely admit the science is 'not done' and have no bias towards the outcome because it's based on experimental data and how you feel about is a non-issue. Yay, science.

But then you started talking about Philosophy, Women's Studies, Sociology, and English. Those are subjective. So within the framework of the Dunning-Kruger effect, when someone questions the rate of acceleration of an object at sea level, we're all able to agree on the answer and it's provable by experimentation. On the other hand, feminism will, for example, claim that we live in a 'Rape Culture'. Now, when first I heard that claim I thought to myself how bad that was. I don't want my daughter growing up in a society where according to Wikipedia: rape is pervasive and normalized due to societal attitudes about gender and sexuality. Who would?

Now I'm not a Women's Studies student, but I am a male (who would be doing the raping) and I do interact as a highly social individual with a large number of male and female friends across a broad socio-economic spectrum, and I can assure you rape is neither pervasive or normalized in those circles. I can easily point out the high profile rape cases which have been presented in the media which led to extensive damage to the accused well before any legal proceedings began indicating that rape is neither normalized or pervasive based on public reaction alone.

So, with regards specifically to Dunning-Krugar. I would say that there is an argument to be made that those who you would traditionally consider to be experts on a subject (professors, spokespeople, etc) specifically in the area of Women's Studies, or Sociology, who may believe themselves to be experts in that they are familiar with all the presented studies, sound bites, authors, theories, etc, may be the ones who falsely believe their knowledge to be superior. The thing that is truly alarming about these disciplines is that there is little science and lots of opinion, and huge amounts of hostility (which has no useful place in public discourse) towards ideas which go against currently held popular opinion.

Few people arrive at anti-feminist views over a single article. Often they do read. They do discuss. And then when they disagree they are attacked, shouted down, belittled, and shamed. I KNOW without taking courses that feminism has worked to pass a number of measures which discriminate against men in ways they would not allow themselves to be discriminated against. 'Manspreading' laws. The tender years doctrine. How rape accusations are being handled on campuses. I KNOW that a nobel prize winning scientist was asked to step down or forced out of his various positions because of a joke he made, and I KNOW that a woman who tweets under #killallwhitemen did not. I KNOW that misandry is a joke and men can't be legally raped by a woman. I KNOW that often quoted statistics about rape and the wage gap have been disproven.

So there are two options. The actual experts are lying and/or not experts at all, OR, I'm wrong. If I'm wrong that's not my fault. I have looked at both sides and what I know is that if you disagree with feminist talking points you're a shitlord, or a rape apologist, or a neckbeard, or something derogatory, but one thing I'm not is being convinced that I'm wrong by facts and logic. So.... Dunning-Kruger and feminism? I honestly don't think the real experts are experts, because they appear to be making it up. It's not science, it's opinion.

TL;DR: Feminism isn't science, it's fiction.

You've taken "subjective" and used it as a synonym for "worthless". You have no reason to believe that you have a natural understanding of any subjective discipline, and no reason to believe that your unresearched opinions are worthwhile. You've fallen into the very trap I outlined. It's not your fault that you're wrong, but it is your fault to think that your ignorance trumps others' knowledge.

I used a folded piece as a handle for a box that had broken. It was virtually unbreakable and as long as it didn't crumple wouldn't hurt your hand.

I have used it for a number of things. In a pinch you can make a watertight(ish) container for carrying water. Hello all who are viewing (all two of us woot!), I'd like to ask those whom it may concern whether they use weapons in the studio they attend. A simple question it may seem but in my studio Iv'e never seen anybody practicing weapons or heard of us teaching any weapons forms, so it came as a shock to me when I visited friends studios and saw that many students practiced weapons combat regularly. So really I'd like to hear if anybody out there is on the weapons or non weapons side of the practice, and if they know how common it is.

My studio doesn't practice weapons as a matter of course, but we have explored some techniques from GumDO briefly. I personally cross train in Ninjutsu, which means I get all the weapons I could ever want :-)

Yeah gumdo seems interesting, although hows your experience with ninjutsu? Every time I see it advertised I'm always incredibly skeptical. My thoughts are usually that its just there to cash in on ninjutsu's reputation and lure in newbies. But it seems your experience is different. Whats your training look like and is there a specific style or line of studios you train in?

I train with a Bunjinkan master, which means that he had to fly to Japan for every belt starting with fifth dan. If you go with the Bunjinkan there is a pretty strict quality control system, and they should have a certificate signed by Dr. Hatsumi. Of course it will be in Japanese (which I don't read).

"Traditionally" Taekwondo does not include any weapons training.

However, more and more schools incorporate weapons because they:

  • are fun

  • develop hand-eye co-ordination

  • are flashy and impressive to watch

  • are fun

All the weapons that you commonly see in Taekwondo schools have non-TKD origins (mostly Japanese or Chinese, but Escrima is also pretty popular).

My school includes weapons training in the curriculum as well as extracurricularly, but we are not purely a TKD school.
